stops.name: Samarkand, the Sultan's capital: the citadel's last stand
stops.campa: The Shah's greatest city, walled and heavily garrisoned, surrenders its outer town within days when the notables open the gates over the objections of the soldiers still willing to fight; the citadel holds two thousand men a little longer before it too is stormed. Chinggis Khan reviews the artisans of the fallen city and spares every weaver, smith, and mason with a trade to be marched east and put to work in Mongolia and China; the rest of the population is driven out, counted, and divided among the army quarter by quarter as plunder.

stops.name: Nishapur: Tolui's revenge, three pyramids of skulls
stops.campa: When Chinggis Khan's son-in-law Toquchar dies of a stray arrow before Nishapur's walls, the khan's own widowed daughter is granted the city outright to do with as she wishes. Under Tolui's command the population, which had already surrendered once and then revolted, is put to the sword down to the cats and dogs, the Persian chroniclers say, and the skulls of men, women, and children stacked in three separate pyramids so that none could later claim how many of each had died. It stands in every later account as the single most total of the Khwarezmian destructions.

stops.name: Urgench, the brothers' quarrel and the river turned against the ruins
stops.campa: At Gurganj, richest city of Khwarezm, Jochi's offer of surrender terms, meant to spare a capital he already half-considers his own future inheritance, enrages Chagatai, who wants nothing but its destruction; Chinggis Khan ends the quarrel by giving neither son the command, handing it instead to his even-tempered third son, Ögedei. The city falls only after street fighting worse than any other siege of the war; the dikes of the Amu Darya are broken and its waters turned loose into the ruins, drowning what fire and sword had left standing.

stops.name: Persia, Rey and Hamadan burned in the Shah's flight
stops.campa: Sent in the first months of the war to run the fleeing Shah Muhammad to ground, Jebe and Subutai's two tümens follow him the length of Persia, sacking Rey, Qazvin, and Hamadan in his wake, though the Shah himself dies alone and unransomed on a Caspian island before they can reach him. Rather than turn home once their quarry is dead, the two generals ask leave to press on and see something more of the western world before returning, the true beginning of a raid that will outlast the war that sent it and cover more ground than any cavalry action in history.

stops.name: Ganja and the Eldiguzid lands of Azerbaijan
stops.campa: From Nakhichevan and Ardabil the tümens turn into Arran, driving Atabeg Uzbek and his Eldiguzid court out of Ganja itself, the walled city of silk and bazaars where, a generation before, the poet Nizami had built his whole five imagined worlds without once leaving his own gate. The Mongols take the city's ransom rather than storm its walls outright and pass on toward the Kur valley and Georgia, leaving Ganja plundered but not razed; the poet's tomb, already twelve years old on the Baku road, stands through a raid his sheltered lifetime never had to imagine.

stops.name: Georgia, the rout at Khunan
stops.campa: King George IV of Georgia, veteran of Crusade talk with the Pope and lord of a kingdom near the height of its medieval power, gathers his knights to meet the raiders and is broken twice, the second time at Khunan with heavy loss among the Georgian nobility. The tümens do not linger to besiege Tbilisi itself; two lightning defeats are enough to leave the kingdom reeling for a generation, a preview, though no one yet reads it as one, of the full invasion still thirteen years off.

stops.name: The Kalka River, the coalition broken
stops.campa: Turning north through the Caucasus passes and around the Caspian's western shore, the two generals draw a coalition of Cuman and Rus' princes into the open steppe beyond the Dnieper. A false retreat of nine days lures the Rus' host across the Kalka; the Mongols turn and destroy an army many times their own number, killing six princes and, by one report, banqueting on boards laid literally over the bodies of the captured commanders. His part of the raid finished, Subutai turns the tümens east for the four-thousand-mile ride home to report to a khan who is, at that same hour, fighting in the valley of the Indus.

stops.name: The Indus, Jalal ad-Din's leap
stops.campa: Jalal ad-Din, the Shah's son, has already beaten one Mongol column at Parwan and gathers the last free army of Khwarezm on the Indus's western bank; Chinggis Khan closes a crescent of tümens around him, his reserve held back to seal the trap. When the line breaks, Jalal ad-Din spurs his horse over the bluff into the river in full armor and swims the current alive to the far bank, the one commander of the whole war the khan will say he wished his own sons resembled. Watching from the heights, he forbids the archers to shoot at a man swimming for his life, admiring what he cannot catch.

stops.name: The Amu Darya camp, the sage and the medicine of long life
stops.campa: Two years before, from his camp near Samarkand, the khan had written east to Shandong summoning the Taoist master Qiu Chuji, Changchun, 'Eternal Spring,' saying Heaven, angered at China's luxury, had raised a plainer man in its place. The seventy-two-year-old sage crosses the Gobi and the Tien Shan and reaches the Amu Darya camp in spring, received with honor and seated above the generals. Asked for the medicine of immortality, he answers there is none, only a discipline of few desires that keeps a life clean; the khan, more struck than offended, keeps him through the winter as teacher, though he adopts none of the discipline himself.
stops.quote: Adept, what medicine of long life have you brought me from afar?
stops.quote_source: The Travels of an Alchemist (Xiyouji), tr. Arthur Waley, the audience of Chinggis Khan and Qiu Chuji, 1222

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen: rest, and the plan against Xi Xia
stops.campa: After seven years in the west the khan turns his tümens home across the whole breadth of Asia, reaching his own headquarters at Avarga on the Kherlen, a cluster of felt palaces, forges, and grain-pits, seat of the Great Mongol Nation since the kurultai. Past sixty now, he rests among his own herds for the first time in years, receiving the tribute of a world he has spent a decade rearranging, and turns his attention to the one campaign left unfinished at his own back door: the Tangut kingdom of Xi Xia, which sent no troops for the western war and must now answer for it.

stops.name: Xi Xia, the last campaign opens
stops.campa: In the dead of winter the tümens cross the frozen Yellow River and take the Tangut cities one by one: Heisui, Ganzhou, Suzhou, while the khan, no longer young, still directs the campaign from the saddle. The Tangut king Weiming Dewang dies before the war is over; his heir Mozhu holds the mountain fastness around the capital Zhongxing under the Helan range while the countryside is stripped and burned, buying time that will not save the kingdom, the last independent state to stand against the Mongol nation in its own founder's lifetime.

stops.name: The Ordos steppe, the fall from the horse
stops.campa: Hunting wild kulan on the open plain near the front, the khan's horse shies at a herd bolting across his path and throws him hard; he is carried back to camp in great pain. Against his officers' urging to break off the campaign for the winter and let him heal, he insists that a khan's word once given to punish the Tangut cannot be turned back for a fall from a horse, and that retreat now would only teach the enemy that his sickness was weakness. He fights on through the winter, though the pain and the fever that follow never fully leave him again.
